articles.title: Is It Really Rude to Ask Who Else Is Coming Before You RSVP?
articles.content:
An extended family member once made an accidental enemy of my 3-year-old son by giving him clothes for his birthday. Like many little kids, he was a nudist at heart and didn’t consider clothes a gift so much as a punishment. (This child used to call pants “leg jails.”) So when we showed up to the family party later that year, he took one look at said relative and announced at the top of his lungs: “NOT YOU AGAIN—I HATE THIS PARTY.” Clearly, it would have been useful for him to know the guest list in advance (if he could read, which he couldn’t). But he was just saying out loud what many adults have found themselves thinking in various social situations.
Take, for example, a friend of mine who throws a massive holiday party every year. It’s a Kardashian-level event, if the Kardashians lived in suburbia and wore Anthropologie. We’re talking well over 100 invitees. The guest list probably needs its own zip code. I usually know maybe 20 of them. Thankfully, though, she sends the invite through Facebook, which means I can see exactly who has RSVP’d. I’m not proud of this, but I check it. Repeatedly. Like a day trader watching a stock. If a good chunk of my people are on the “Going” list, I’m in, and I will even put on real pants. If it’s a sea of strangers and one lady I once nodded at in a parking lot, I suddenly remember I might have a thing that night.
Does the guest list influence my decision? Absolutely. Do I feel guilty about it? Also absolutely. I should want to go for the hostess, shouldn’t I? She’s wonderful. Her party is wonderful. Supporting my friend should be reason enough. Instead, I’m evaluating her guest list like a Google review page.
But before you judge me, admit it: You do this too. Everybody does this. Nobody commits to a party completely blind, and anyone who claims otherwise is either lying or has better self-esteem than I do. The real etiquette question is what to do when the guest list isn’t conveniently posted on the invite. Is it rude to just ask the host, straight up, “So who else is coming?” I have thought about this far more than a grown woman should. Here’s where I landed.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more etiquette, holidays, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
Everyone wants to know who’s coming. It’s just human nature. The only difference is whether you ask or quietly stalk the RSVP list like it’s an ex’s Instagram. Asking the host is just the honest version of what we’re all doing anyway.
Going to a party takes real effort: the clothes, the sitter, the drive, the small talk, the dessert you bring that you put on a fancy plate hoping no one will notice you got it from the grocery store. Wanting to know whether you’ll see a friendly face at the party isn’t snobbery—it’s basic risk assessment, and the host is the one person who has the answer.
And sometimes, it’s about more than whether the company is fun. I don’t know about you, but if an ex or an ex-friend might be there, I’d at least like a little warning before I walk in.
This question is so awkward. How do you even start that conversation? A party isn’t a menu, and your friend isn’t a waiter. Asking who else is coming can sound like you’re ranking their party, and the host might hear, “I’ll only show up if the cool people do.” Nobody wants to feel like their party is the backup plan.
It can also put the host on the spot. She invited you because she likes you, and now she’s reciting names like a court bailiff while wondering if she’s passing some kind of friendship test.
But the biggest issue is that you risk making the host feel unimportant to you, or at least less important than those other people. Because you are literally telling her that she’s not reason enough for you to attend. Ouch.
Yet, as awkward as it feels, asking who’s coming isn’t the rude part. What you do next is. The rude part is the limbo where you check “maybe” (or nothing at all) on the RSVP list and let days or weeks go by while waiting to see who else is coming. Meanwhile, your host is just trying to figure out the head count she needs for food, chairs and her own sanity. Hosts aren’t mind readers, and “I’ll let you know” without ever letting them know is so rude.
Part of why we stall is that we’re scared to say no. A 2023 study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology found that 77% of people admitted to accepting an invitation they didn’t want because they feared the consequences of declining. Across five experiments, though, people consistently overestimated how upset the host would be. Turns out, the host cares less about the “no” than we think—they just want an answer one way or the other.
That means a quick, gracious “no” is a gift. A “yes” when you back out at the last minute is not.
Hugely. Let’s go through the usual suspects.
Holiday and office parties. It’s party season, so let’s start here. These are “show up, be pleasant, eat three meatballs and don’t get drunk in front of your co-workers” events, and most of the time the guest list shouldn’t decide whether you go. Often, you’re going for a bigger purpose like family traditions or work culture. So go, wave at the people you need to wave at, and perfect your exit strategy.
Weddings. The list is set, the caterer has your name and you’re there for the couple. Asking who’s coming is mostly pointless. The one exception is a genuine feud that requires seating-chart diplomacy, and that’s a conversation for the couple, not a reason to hold your RSVP. But even in that case, I’d advise you to tread carefully, as your private life is not their problem to solve.
Kids’ parties. Totally fine to ask. “Will anyone from his class be there?” is parenting logistics, not social climbing. Also, carpools.
Intimate dinners. This is where it gets dicey. If there are only eight people at the table, the host hand-picked each one, and asking for names feels like you’re vetting her friends. With a close friend, a casual question is fine. (Heck, it’s probably on the group chat.) With an acquaintance, just RSVP.
Family events. You can ask whether Uncle Rick is coming. You can’t use the answer as a way out, just as advance warning to prepare yourself. And remember: You love these people (hopefully), and that’s the point.
Any event where your ex might be. Ask. But ask the host privately and directly, and ask for information, not for them to rescind his invitation. If you can’t be in the same room as someone, a polite “no” is always available. Do not make them mediate your conflict.
First, check whether the list is already visible on the invite. If it isn’t, ask the host directly, and frame it as logistics, not a vibe check. Try, “Count me in! Who else is going? I’m figuring out who to carpool with.” Or the sneakier version: “Is it a big crowd or more of a small thing?” You get the information without making the host recite a roster.
Timing matters too. Ask when the invite lands or in the same message as your RSVP. Don’t let the indecision go on forever, which is important with all RSVPs, regardless of this situation.
Whatever you do, don’t text a mutual friend or group chat to ask who’s going, because you may accidentally reveal that someone wasn’t invited. And then you’ve created a whole new etiquette problem for this column. Go to the source.
It is not rude to ask the host who else is coming. Everyone wants to know; you’re just the one brave enough to say it out loud. What’s rude is holding your answer hostage until you like what you hear.
My ruling: If it is truly that important to you, ask your question, get your answer and RSVP within a couple of days. If the guest list is a deal-breaker, send a kind “no.” If it’s not, say “yes” and bring your best attitude.
And if you do end up in a sea of strangers, the holiday-party basics still apply: Find the host, say hello and say goodbye. Do the small talk. Eat the treats. You might even make a new friend—perhaps someone else who thinks pants are leg jails.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE! Regina King Talks About Her Next Chapter and Finding New Meaning in Holiday Traditions
articles.content:
Regina King is only 55 years old, but because she started acting professionally at 14, she already boasts an impressive four-decade body of work across film and TV. And if you look at some of her biggest roles thus far—from supportive mother Sharon Rivers in If Beale Street Could Talk (which won her an Oscar in 2019) to business-savvy, heart-forward wife Marcee Tidwell in her breakout, Jerry Maguire, to detective Lydia Adams in the five-season crime drama Southland to detective/vigilante/mother Angela Abar in HBO’s Watchmen limited series (which earned her an Emmy in 2020)—there’s a key character trait that surfaces: She’s often a protector.
I present King with that idea when we sit down for down for a conversationin late July. “I’ve never heard anyone point to protection as a through line,” she says, running all her roles through her mind. “I think … that’s a bit of me. Who I am.”
When we talk, King is in New York City to celebrate the release of the trailer of her upcoming film, Children of Blood and Bone, a fantasy epic based on the book series by Tomi Adeyemi. In the film (out Jan. 15), King plays Queen Nehanda, mother of Prince Inan and Princess Amari, in the kingdom of Orïsha, where magic has been violently suppressed.
Motherhood—and daughterhood—end up being a lot of what King and I discuss. Midlife often brings the combination of great achievement and profound loss. Over the last decade(ish), King has received four Emmys and one Oscar, and released her critically adored directorial debut—2020’s One Night in Miami. But personally, she’s living with epic grief. Her only son, Ian Desduné, died in January 2022, at age 26. Since then, King has not shied away from talking about him and her experiences these past few years—in fact, Ian came up within the first minute of our conversation.
King is determined to keep Ian a part of her present—and future. In 2025, she launched her wine label, MianU, in his honor. “It was Ian who first introduced me to orange wine,” she wrote on Instagram. “Inspired by [his] deep love for art, flavor and the people around him, I created a wine that celebrates the beauty of connection.”
Winemaking is another new experience to add to her stacked résumé—and one she sometimes dreams about pursuing full time. But for the moment, there’s still a lot of on-screen work she wants to do, she assures me over lunch. Here’s an excerpt of our conversation.
This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
I feel like I’m always growing. And this reality of life without Ian is a whole new beginning in a lot of ways. I’m a different person navigating it. I’m at an age and at a place of having such experience that I have to know that God is evenly and equally everywhere all the time. And life is all of it—the devastation brings you to the next beginning.
When I look at each of those stages, I realize—and I want to speak for myself—how many things aren’t calculated. Like, I always wanted to be a mother, and I always wanted to be an actor. But you don’t know what that’s going to look like. As it was happening, I didn’t know that I would be posed with the question of going through a divorce or having to say no to a lot of roles because I couldn’t be traveling. When Ian was of school age, I couldn’t take him out of school.
And so if that hadn’t happened, I would have never, as an actor, found my way to Southland. I can give you a ton of life-changing moments like that, which inform the woman that you’re sitting in front of right now. But I guess to put it all into one thing: I’m very aware of how life is guiding—and I’m still remaining open to follow.
Yeah, it’s interesting because I had Ian at 25. But also at 25, I had been a working actor for 11 years. So I felt more grown than I probably was.
Honestly, my mother keeping me in public school made such a difference. I knew that I was a celebrity kid. But I didn’t hang around celebrity kids. Tichina Arnold and Tisha Campbell? I knew them, because I would see them on auditions, but we didn’t become friends until we were in our 20s.
Once I started 227, I’d go to school on set, and that teacher corresponds with your teachers at school. So I’d keep up with the work but get ahead, because it would just be me in class. And then [when we weren’t filming] I’d come back to school. And since I was ahead, I could just run track and do all of the things that all the other kids did.
We couldn’t say that we didn’t like something if we didn’t try it. With everything, from food to music to reading a book. So: not to give a judgment on something without experiencing it first. I would say that’s a pretty big one.
My mother always supported all of the things that my sister Reina and I wanted to do—we would just have to finish whatever she was signing us up for. And at one point, we ran into my mother’s friend, who lived down the street from Todd Bridges’s mother, who was an acting teacher. So we started going to [Betty Bridges’s] acting class, doing plays, and that became way more interesting to me than ballet or tap class.
My sister and I, before that, we used to recite poetry for our parents or for anyone that was coming over. My mom had gotten us plays for young adults, and so we would put on plays too. The idea of being able to play someone else, believably, was like an “aha!” But it was a hobby. I wanted to be a dentist.
I loved my childhood dentist growing up. He made the importance of teeth being clean clear, and made me just pay attention to mouths more than eyes. That was fascinating to me. But I didn’t really factor in that I would have to be, like, in people’s mouths. [laughs]
In this movie, I play a queen who’s concerned about the well-being of her son. She loves being part of the royal family. I haven’t seen a story like this where the main character is a young girl who’s both strong and soft. You get to see her fall in love, you get to see her kick ass. As an audience member, when I watched it, I just felt like, Oh, we haven’t had one of these in a long time. Girl power, you know what I mean?
Because it’s Ian. It’s a passion. It’s, like, we’re doing this, Ian. Let’s go. I’m still learning with it all the time. Which is exciting. I would like to be in Mendocino, California, even more, at the farms where my grapes are coming from, to be able to really talk to those farmers, about the grapes and what’s gonna be the best vintage for next year. But there are not enough hours in the day.
Right now, I’m terrible with that, I’m not even gonna lie. I’m not doing anything steadily, really, except for every Thursday and Saturday when I light a candle with Ian and talk with him. I used to be a person who would have my morning cup of tea. Now I only do it on Saturday when I’m sitting outside and having that moment with him.
As far as ritual things that I do and have done, working out is a big one. We lost our last dog about eight months ago. And our dogs werebig dogs, so I was always walking, at the minimum, a couple miles a day. Now that I’ve stopped walking, I can feel it.
Traveling makes working out hard, but I find if I get a good two weeks at home, where I’m on it, I feel such a difference. I have to give myself [the pep talk], you know: Regina, if it’s 20 minutes, that’s movement.
My mom is 82. And watching her decline definitely makes me want to be more active.
For so much of my life, I thought that emotions were all separate. But they’re happening in concert—happy and sad at the same time. There was a time where I couldn’t even breathe, you know? But, of course, I could breathe.
I want to feel him physically, but to feel him on a spiritual level … I wouldn’t be able to survive if I couldn’t be open to knowing what that feels like. I never know how Ian is gonna present [himself to me]. And I’m finding the joy in not knowing when those little moments are gonna show up.
I’m still defining. Thanksgiving? I leave the country. Because so much of Thanksgiving is wrapped around us cooking together, and that’s never gonna happen again, so why try to duplicate it?
We lost my stepdad, Fred, the year after Ian, so it’s now me, my sisters—my sister, Reina, and my stepsister, Stephanie Darby, who I call my “bonus sister”—and my mother, and for the last three Christmases, we’ve spent it together in California at my house. That’s been good for us. We cook, we go to museums, sometimes we just stay in three or four days straight. It looks different; it feels new. And we tell stories about Fred and Ian.
So many of my memories are wrapped up in the time between October and January. So sometime in October, I start getting this feeling—the absences are louder than at other times of the year. Last year, I remember feeling so hollow. Your body knows. Your body has that inner journal.
But I have a wonderful man in my life who I know Ian’s spirit definitely played a part in summoning to take care of his mom. And he always reminds me not to apologize for the tears when they come, no matter who I’m with, no matter what. So I just let them come, and people react, and I just let them react and it’s just … this is what’s happening. It’s life.
Very much. But I think it’s talked about more in other cultures. It’s different than in American culture.
Yeah, totally. So I hope this makes you laugh as much as it did to me. It made me wanna cry at the same time. My mother is coming to Los Angeles to live with me for a month. So, in preparation for her coming, I’ve been checking out senior centers, looking at their monthly schedules and seeing what they have to offer so she can visit and socialize while she’s there. We take our mom to a senior center for exercise classes in Cincinnati [where she lives], but I’ve never really done any research on the centers in L.A.
So I went to this one and asked about the age range. And the person I spoke with said, “Well, the sign-up age begins at 55.” And I was like, “So you’re saying I can join the senior center with my mom?” I was like, “Well, if I sign up, too, is it at least a yearly discount for family? A family rate?” [laughs]
I’m still doing a lot of what I’ve done in the past, which is going by my gut. My good old gut. It’s interesting—as a producer, you can put so much time into things that don’t ever make it. I’ve experienced that a lot. But then there are some things that, 12 years later, finally happened.
My faith really was challenged, losing Ian. The things that I’ve said publicly all came in question for me, like: God is good all the time. All the time, God is good. Like, those type of affirmations that I have said and believed were challenged. What surprised me the most is that, in that period of doubt, faith was still acting subconsciously, and was still keeping me in.
And I’m also surprised at just how open I’ve been through it all. Just me saying that to you out loud that I’m not OK or wasn’t OK, is surprising because I’ve been very conscious in my life to be private. So to recognize that I’m totally allowed to have that struggle and to say it out loud is a surprising thing. Someone else will probably be like, “Girl, that is nothing.” But it’s huge for me.

Over the last decade(ish), King has received four Emmys and one Oscar, and released her critically adored directorial debut—2020’s One Night in Miami. But personally, she’s living with epic grief. Her only son, Ian Desduné, died in January 2022, at age 26. Since then, King has not shied away from talking about him and her experiences these past few years—in fact, Ian came up within the first minute of our conversation.

King is determined to keep Ian a part of her present—and future. In 2025, she launched her wine label, MianU, in his honor. “It was Ian who first introduced me to orange wine,” she wrote on Instagram. “Inspired by [his] deep love for art, flavor and the people around him, I created a wine that celebrates the beauty of connection.”

Winemaking is another new experience to add to her stacked résumé—and one she sometimes dreams about pursuing full time. But for the moment, there’s still a lot of on-screen work she wants to do, she assures me over lunch. Here’s an excerpt of our conversation.

This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Tell me a little about where you find yourself in life right now.

I feel like I’m always growing. And this reality of life without Ian is a whole new beginning in a lot of ways. I’m a different person navigating it. I’m at an age and at a place of having such experience that I have to know that God is evenly and equally everywhere all the time. And life is all of it—the devastation brings you to the next beginning.

When I look at each of those stages, I realize—and I want to speak for myself—how many things aren’t calculated. Like, I always wanted to be a mother, and I always wanted to be an actor. But you don’t know what that’s going to look like. As it was happening, I didn’t know that I would be posed with the question of going through a divorce or having to say no to a lot of roles because I couldn’t be traveling. When Ian was of school age, I couldn’t take him out of school.

And so if that hadn’t happened, I would have never, as an actor, found my way to Southland. I can give you a ton of life-changing moments like that, which inform the woman that you’re sitting in front of right now. But I guess to put it all into one thing: I’m very aware of how life is guiding—and I’m still remaining open to follow.

That makes me think of when you’re little and you’re asked: “What do you want to be when you grow up?” And you have the story of what you want your life to be—but then you get to midlife and you see what the story actually ended up being.

Yeah, it’s interesting because I had Ian at 25. But also at 25, I had been a working actor for 11 years. So I felt more grown than I probably was.

Your first big role was on TV as Brenda Jenkins on 227. You were 14 when that show hit prime time. But when people talk about your career, you don’t often hear the term child star, though you were a child star to a certain extent. What was that experience like—and how did you keep your feet on the ground?

Honestly, my mother keeping me in public school made such a difference. I knew that I was a celebrity kid. But I didn’t hang around celebrity kids. Tichina Arnold and Tisha Campbell? I knew them, because I would see them on auditions, but we didn’t become friends until we were in our 20s.

Once I started 227, I’d go to school on set, and that teacher corresponds with your teachers at school. So I’d keep up with the work but get ahead, because it would just be me in class. And then [when we weren’t filming] I’d come back to school. And since I was ahead, I could just run track and do all of the things that all the other kids did.

What were the values in your house?

We couldn’t say that we didn’t like something if we didn’t try it. With everything, from food to music to reading a book. So: not to give a judgment on something without experiencing it first. I would say that’s a pretty big one.

How did you get into acting?

My mother always supported all of the things that my sister Reina and I wanted to do—we would just have to finish whatever she was signing us up for. And at one point, we ran into my mother’s friend, who lived down the street from Todd Bridges’s mother, who was an acting teacher. So we started going to [Betty Bridges’s] acting class, doing plays, and that became way more interesting to me than ballet or tap class.

My sister and I, before that, we used to recite poetry for our parents or for anyone that was coming over. My mom had gotten us plays for young adults, and so we would put on plays too. The idea of being able to play someone else, believably, was like an “aha!” But it was a hobby. I wanted to be a dentist.

A dentist?!

I loved my childhood dentist growing up. He made the importance of teeth being clean clear, and made me just pay attention to mouths more than eyes. That was fascinating to me. But I didn’t really factor in that I would have to be, like, in people’s mouths. [laughs]

You’re here not as a dentist but to talk about your role in Children of Blood and Bone. What drew you to the role?

In this movie, I play a queen who’s concerned about the well-being of her son. She loves being part of the royal family. I haven’t seen a story like this where the main character is a young girl who’s both strong and soft. You get to see her fall in love, you get to see her kick ass. As an audience member, when I watched it, I just felt like, Oh, we haven’t had one of these in a long time. Girl power, you know what I mean?

You’ve added a wine label, MianU, to an already very busy schedule. What made you jump into it?

Because it’s Ian. It’s a passion. It’s, like, we’re doing this, Ian. Let’s go. I’m still learning with it all the time. Which is exciting. I would like to be in Mendocino, California, even more, at the farms where my grapes are coming from, to be able to really talk to those farmers, about the grapes and what’s gonna be the best vintage for next year. But there are not enough hours in the day.

You travel a lot for your job. What are the things that you do every day or every week to keep yourself steady amid everything else changing?

Right now, I’m terrible with that, I’m not even gonna lie. I’m not doing anything steadily, really, except for every Thursday and Saturday when I light a candle with Ian and talk with him. I used to be a person who would have my morning cup of tea. Now I only do it on Saturday when I’m sitting outside and having that moment with him.

As far as ritual things that I do and have done, working out is a big one. We lost our last dog about eight months ago. And our dogs werebig dogs, so I was always walking, at the minimum, a couple miles a day. Now that I’ve stopped walking, I can feel it.

Traveling makes working out hard, but I find if I get a good two weeks at home, where I’m on it, I feel such a difference. I have to give myself [the pep talk], you know: Regina, if it’s 20 minutes, that’s movement.

My mom is 82. And watching her decline definitely makes me want to be more active.

Yes. I understand that from my experience with my dad at the end of his life. It can be a motivator to try to really be active and present. On that note, part of what’s so inspiring about the way you talk about Ian is that you keep him in the present tense. Can you talk a bit about living through that experience so publicly?

For so much of my life, I thought that emotions were all separate. But they’re happening in concert—happy and sad at the same time. There was a time where I couldn’t even breathe, you know? But, of course, I could breathe.

I want to feel him physically, but to feel him on a spiritual level … I wouldn’t be able to survive if I couldn’t be open to knowing what that feels like. I never know how Ian is gonna present [himself to me]. And I’m finding the joy in not knowing when those little moments are gonna show up.

You have some wonderful videos on the MianU website with your sister talking about the challenge of the holidays after living through loss. How, in the past couple of years, have you redefined what this time of year means for you?

I’m still defining. Thanksgiving? I leave the country. Because so much of Thanksgiving is wrapped around us cooking together, and that’s never gonna happen again, so why try to duplicate it?

We lost my stepdad, Fred, the year after Ian, so it’s now me, my sisters—my sister, Reina, and my stepsister, Stephanie Darby, who I call my “bonus sister”—and my mother, and for the last three Christmases, we’ve spent it together in California at my house. That’s been good for us. We cook, we go to museums, sometimes we just stay in three or four days straight. It looks different; it feels new. And we tell stories about Fred and Ian.

So many of my memories are wrapped up in the time between October and January. So sometime in October, I start getting this feeling—the absences are louder than at other times of the year. Last year, I remember feeling so hollow. Your body knows. Your body has that inner journal.

But I have a wonderful man in my life who I know Ian’s spirit definitely played a part in summoning to take care of his mom. And he always reminds me not to apologize for the tears when they come, no matter who I’m with, no matter what. So I just let them come, and people react, and I just let them react and it’s just … this is what’s happening. It’s life.

It’s a gift you give other people, though, by being vulnerable. Because grief touches everybody. And it’s a hard thing to talk about.

Very much. But I think it’s talked about more in other cultures. It’s different than in American culture.

That’s true. And it used to be more common to have generations of families living in the same house, so there was more of a clear view of life stages.

Yeah, totally. So I hope this makes you laugh as much as it did to me. It made me wanna cry at the same time. My mother is coming to Los Angeles to live with me for a month. So, in preparation for her coming, I’ve been checking out senior centers, looking at their monthly schedules and seeing what they have to offer so she can visit and socialize while she’s there. We take our mom to a senior center for exercise classes in Cincinnati [where she lives], but I’ve never really done any research on the centers in L.A.

So I went to this one and asked about the age range. And the person I spoke with said, “Well, the sign-up age begins at 55.” And I was like, “So you’re saying I can join the senior center with my mom?” I was like, “Well, if I sign up, too, is it at least a yearly discount for family? A family rate?” [laughs]

You said earlier that there aren’t enough hours in the day. How do you make choices about the projects that you give your time to?

I’m still doing a lot of what I’ve done in the past, which is going by my gut. My good old gut. It’s interesting—as a producer, you can put so much time into things that don’t ever make it. I’ve experienced that a lot. But then there are some things that, 12 years later, finally happened.

How have you surprised yourself as an adult?

My faith really was challenged, losing Ian. The things that I’ve said publicly all came in question for me, like: God is good all the time. All the time, God is good. Like, those type of affirmations that I have said and believed were challenged. What surprised me the most is that, in that period of doubt, faith was still acting subconsciously, and was still keeping me in.

And I’m also surprised at just how open I’ve been through it all. Just me saying that to you out loud that I’m not OK or wasn’t OK, is surprising because I’ve been very conscious in my life to be private. So to recognize that I’m totally allowed to have that struggle and to say it out loud is a surprising thing. Someone else will probably be like, “Girl, that is nothing.” But it’s huge for me.

No, I am not talking about Grand Theft Auto VI, though that will be on the menu at my house too. (But not during dinner!) This is a game involving other kinds of missions, ones that are a little more family-friendly. You don’t have to buy anything, and there’s no complicated setup or rules—though you will get points for being clever.

What is the “secret mission” game?

It’s simple. Everyone at your gathering gets a secret task they must complete before the meal or gathering is over. These missions can be silly, sweet, lightly diabolical or totally absurd, but they must be secret. Example: Bring up your neighbor’s cat in three separate conversations. Guests try to figure out what everyone else’s mission is, with a big reveal after the meal.

The secret mission game isn’t new, but social media has recast the party game into a major holiday trend. On Instagram, the top posts have millions of views, and commenters can’t resist sharing their own ideas for missions as well as stories of their family’s hilarious reactions to the game.

  • “This is what we’re doing at Thanksgiving!” said an Instagram user after copying their entire family on the thread.
  • “We played this [last] year,” said someone on TikTok. “My mission was to stack rolls on someone’s plate until they noticed.”
  • “If I had to eat my thanksgiving meal with my left hand I’d crash out 😂,” someone on Instagram said about a particularly difficult mission for righties.
  • “Me writing my own mission: ‘sneak away to nap without anyone noticing’ 🤝💤,” said another Instagram user.

How do you play, exactly?

Secret mission is pretty casual, and your family may develop “house rules,” but here’s the basic structure: Everyone at your gathering gets a piece of paper outlining their secret mission. These can be drawn from a hat as guests walk in the door, or you can give each person their mission at their place setting.

Each guest then must complete their mission by the time dinner is over, dessert is served or whatever time frame you choose. At the reveal, guess each others’ missions or just laugh at everyone’s silly behavior. Depending on your rules, you could give prizes for the best approach or funniest delivery.

But first, the host needs to come up with some great ideas for missions. You’re shooting for lighthearted fun, not discomfort or humiliation, so keep the instructions squarely G-rated. Here are a few missions to get started, culled from around the web:

  • Emphasize every bite with a big “mmmm.”
  • Start a random round of applause for the chef, the turkey or even the dog.
  • Speak in a whisper the entire meal, and feign ignorance when asked about it.
  • Repeatedly say you have an announcement to make, but never make one.
  • Bring up aliens in every conversation.
  • Get two people to say “Oklahoma” or “Willie Nelson” or any other random word or phrase.
  • Repeat what people say back to them while nodding vigorously.

Should you have a game at your Thanksgiving dinner, even if you’re all adults?

Sure! The secret mission game is for any type of guest list. Bonding over a fun shared experience and having a few laughs beats awkwardly commenting on the mashed potatoes with your second cousin you haven’t seen since you were 3—unless that’s your mission, of course. And if you do have kids at the table, they will have a blast seeing adults do silly things.

Even the most comfortable family gatherings and Friendsgivings can get a little stale, conversation-wise, and this game is guaranteed to get people talking and laughing. Plus, it gets people off their phones. Finally, if your family tends to bicker with one another or fight over politics, the secret mission game keeps the focus light.

What are some other games you can play?

Secret mission is just one of many fun group games that are perfect for Thanksgiving, Christmas or any other holiday gathering. Here are some suggestions, plus mini explainers:

  • Two Truths and a Lie. Everyone shares three statements about themselves; people guess which one is false.
  • Celebrity (aka Fishbowl). Teams draw famous names out of a bowl and try to guess them through increasingly difficult clues: full descriptions, single words and acting them out.
  • Who Am I? Players stick famous names to their foreheads, facing out, and ask the other guests a series of questions to figure out who they are.
  • Charades. An oldie but goodie. Players try to get their teammates to guess a person, movie, phrase or activity through nonverbal clues only.

articles.title: This Genius Technique Will Instantly Get You Out of a Conversation That You Can’t Seem to Escape
articles.content:
Whether you’re at a family gathering, a Friendsgiving or an office party, you’re bound to find yourself in a one-on-one you want to escape this holiday season. Your aunt corners you by the cheese board and wants to know why you’re still single. A friend spends 20 minutes walking you through every. single. detail. of her latest situationship. Your co-worker follows you down the entire buffet line, recounting his end-of-year review. You want out, but you stay put—because how do you leave any of these conversations without seeming rude?
If this sounds familiar, you’re not alone. In fact, a 2021 study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found that only about 2% of conversations ended when both people wanted them to. Well, we have the answer to this awkward situation: an expert-recommended technique that’s a lot easier to pull off than you think. Even better? It’s both polite and final.
To master this graceful way out—and also learn how to avoid becoming the person everyone’s trying to ditch—we turned to Adam Mastroianni, PhD, an experimental psychologist and the lead author of the study; Natalie Bernstein, PsyD, a licensed clinical psychologist; and Sabrina Zohar, a relationship coach and the author of Why Am I Like This? Break Your Relationship Patterns and Create the Life You Want.
Read on for the technique you won’t know how you survived without—and memorize this move before your next get-together.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more relationships, holidays, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
Blame it on good manners. Most of us aren’t at a loss for words; we’re just too busy worrying about the other person. “We want out of the conversation, but we don’t want the other person to feel like we’re rejecting them or dismissing them,” Bernstein explains. “We feel bad, because we’re anticipating that they’re going to be disappointed.” And we really don’t want to interrupt someone while they’re talking or, worse, walk away from them mid-sentence.
Plus, for many of us, especially women, the urge to stay put was drilled in early. “We’re taught to go say hi to everybody, be a good girl, don’t ruffle any feathers,” says Zohar. So we do what she calls self-abandoning: We smile and nod to keep everyone else comfortable, “even though internally we might be struggling.”
Even crazier? The person you’re talking to may feel just as trapped as you do. According to Mastroianni’s research, both people are often being polite at the same time. “Neither person wants to offend the other by bailing on the conversation,” he says. “But both people may mistakenly think the other person wants to keep going, when, in fact, everyone is ready to leave.”
The problem is that there isn’t always a graceful off-ramp. “Conversations are a bit like highways: You can’t just leave whenever you want,” Mastroianni says. “You have to wait for the appropriate exit. And that exit might be a few miles down the road, long after you first felt ready to get off the highway.”
It also doesn’t help that we’re terrible at reading one another. In Mastroianni’s study, participants were asked when they had wanted their conversation to end—and to guess when their partner had wanted it to end. On average, their guesses were off by about nine minutes. That’s a big miss, considering the conversations lasted only about 20 minutes on average. In other words, we can misjudge when the other person is ready to go by nearly half the conversation.
Luckily, there’s a smart way out of any awkward, uncomfortable or just plain boring conversation. Bernstein calls it the Connect and Close technique, which boils down to being direct and physically following through.
First, you deliver this magical line: “It was really nice to see you—I’m glad we got a chance to catch up. I’m going to go say hello to a few other people.”
At the same time, you pair it with some very specific body language. “You can look across the room, wave to someone or shift and turn your body a little bit away while you’re saying it,” Bernstein says. “Then they’re getting information not only from your words but also from what they’re seeing.”
Then—and this is the part most of us have the most trouble with—you leave.
Simply put, it’s kind and clear. “You’re acknowledging the time that you spent with them, but then also being direct and moving on,” Bernstein says. Because there’s no ambiguity, the other person isn’t left wondering what just happened. Plus, says Mastroianni, you make the other person feel appreciated, not that you’re “simply fed up with their presence.”
In fact, it’s the long, apologetic exit that’s more likely to sting. “When it’s indirect or there’s too much talking, it gives people room to start thinking, Wait a second—they seem really uncomfortable. Don’t they want to talk to me?” Bernstein says. “If they don’t have that space, they don’t have that thought.”
And if you’re worried that cutting things short will hurt someone’s feelings, the research suggests otherwise. “Going in [to our study], we expected that if a conversation ended before someone wanted it to end, they’d feel pretty bummed. This is not what we found,” Mastroianni says. “If anything, they were the happiest group! It turns out it’s fine to be left wanting more.” His analogy: “Think about finishing a bowl of ice cream: If you want more ice cream, it’s probably because the ice cream was pretty good. If you want less ice cream, it’s probably because your stomach hurts.”
Even with the right words, a few common slip-ups can make the exit more awkward than it needs to be. Here’s what to avoid.
The basic formula works almost anywhere with anyone, but a few small adjustments can help.
At a family gathering: If you’re settled in on the couch, Bernstein says, simply stand up after you deliver the line. Try something like: “It was so good to chat with you. I’m going to go see how Aunt Sally’s doing—I haven’t talked to her in a while.”
When a relative gets nosy: That aunt who wants to know why you’re still single? You don’t owe her an explanation. Zohar suggests turning the spotlight around: “That’s not something I’m comfortable sharing, but let’s talk about you. Tell me about your trip.” It works, she says, because “people love to talk about themselves.”
At a work event: Offer a handshake along with something like: “It was good to see you again. Take care, and have fun tonight,” Bernstein suggests.
With a friend who’s venting: You don’t want to seem dismissive when someone is clearly going through something. Acknowledge what they’re sharing, then suggest a time to continue. “You could say, ‘It certainly sounds like there’s a lot going on. I really do want to hear about it, but unfortunately I have to go. Maybe we can catch up again soon and you can fill me in,'” Bernstein suggests. And if you’re two martinis into your friend’s breakup story, Zohar says it’s OK to validate what they’re going through, then be honest that you don’t have the bandwidth right now. Her take: “Honesty is kindness, and I think a lot of people are scared of that.”
When you truly can’t leave: At a seated holiday dinner, you may not be able to walk across the room. Bernstein recommends having a helpful exit ready, such as: “I’m going to start on the dishes.” Or borrow Zohar’s go-to: “Excuse me for a moment. I’m going to go use the restroom.” Chances are, by the time you return, they’ll have found someone else to unload on. And if someone brings up politics or your love life and you’re stuck at the table? Try to pivot with “I think we’ve talked about that enough—how are you doing?”
You don’t need to avoid them for the rest of the night. If you cross paths again, Bernstein advises keeping it light: “Hey, how are you? Are you having fun tonight?”
If you’re worried about getting pulled right back into an intense conversation, it’s helpful if you take the wheel. Bernstein says her husband, who’s also a psychologist, is a pro at this. He’ll gently shift things to something neutral, like sports teams, holiday travel plans or what everyone’s watching on Netflix. “It’s something more benign that is still a conversation,” she says, “but it doesn’t suck you into that heaviness where people want to share their whole life story with us.”
That said, you can pick the conversation back up later if you want to. As Mastroianni says, “We always have the option of speaking more in the future, but we never have the option of speaking less than we already did.”
The Connect and Close should be your go-to, but it helps to have a few backup moves ready, especially when the usual exit isn’t an option.
It happens to the best of us, especially when we’re excited about what we’re saying. Bernstein suggests checking for these signs that the other person is ready to move on.
If you suspect you’ve overstayed your welcome—or you want to avoid that possibility—try these moves.
No. But if it feels like you’re itching to get away from everyone you talk to, Mastroianni suggests turning the lens on yourself. “Are you being a good conversation partner? Are you paying attention? Are you looking for what’s interesting about the other person?” he says. “Some people are bores, sure, and for those folks, you’ll have to politely excuse yourself eventually. But anyone can be made boring by the way you treat them.”
His research also suggests that our dread is often overblown. Most of the conversations in his study were highly enjoyable to both people, even when they didn’t end sooner. “People are way too anxious about their conversations,” he says. “Over and over again, we find that people fear them beforehand, enjoy them while they’re going on and then completely forget and go back to fearing them again.”

Whether you’re at a family gathering, a Friendsgiving or an office party, you’re bound to find yourself in a one-on-one you want to escape this holiday season. Your aunt corners you by the cheese board and wants to know why you’re still single. A friend spends 20 minutes walking you through every. single. detail. of her latest situationship. Your co-worker follows you down the entire buffet line, recounting his end-of-year review. You want out, but you stay put—because how do you leave any of these conversations without seeming rude?

If this sounds familiar, you’re not alone. In fact, a 2021 study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found that only about 2% of conversations ended when both people wanted them to. Well, we have the answer to this awkward situation: an expert-recommended technique that’s a lot easier to pull off than you think. Even better? It’s both polite and final.

To master this graceful way out—and also learn how to avoid becoming the person everyone’s trying to ditch—we turned to Adam Mastroianni, PhD, an experimental psychologist and the lead author of the study; Natalie Bernstein, PsyD, a licensed clinical psychologist; and Sabrina Zohar, a relationship coach and the author of Why Am I Like This? Break Your Relationship Patterns and Create the Life You Want.

Read on for the technique you won’t know how you survived without—and memorize this move before your next get-together.

Why do we feel so paralyzed when we’re trapped in a conversation?

Blame it on good manners. Most of us aren’t at a loss for words; we’re just too busy worrying about the other person. “We want out of the conversation, but we don’t want the other person to feel like we’re rejecting them or dismissing them,” Bernstein explains. “We feel bad, because we’re anticipating that they’re going to be disappointed.” And we really don’t want to interrupt someone while they’re talking or, worse, walk away from them mid-sentence.

Plus, for many of us, especially women, the urge to stay put was drilled in early. “We’re taught to go say hi to everybody, be a good girl, don’t ruffle any feathers,” says Zohar. So we do what she calls self-abandoning: We smile and nod to keep everyone else comfortable, “even though internally we might be struggling.”

Even crazier? The person you’re talking to may feel just as trapped as you do. According to Mastroianni’s research, both people are often being polite at the same time. “Neither person wants to offend the other by bailing on the conversation,” he says. “But both people may mistakenly think the other person wants to keep going, when, in fact, everyone is ready to leave.”

The problem is that there isn’t always a graceful off-ramp. “Conversations are a bit like highways: You can’t just leave whenever you want,” Mastroianni says. “You have to wait for the appropriate exit. And that exit might be a few miles down the road, long after you first felt ready to get off the highway.”

It also doesn’t help that we’re terrible at reading one another. In Mastroianni’s study, participants were asked when they had wanted their conversation to end—and to guess when their partner had wanted it to end. On average, their guesses were off by about nine minutes. That’s a big miss, considering the conversations lasted only about 20 minutes on average. In other words, we can misjudge when the other person is ready to go by nearly half the conversation.

What’s the phrase that will get you out of a conversation politely but definitively?

Luckily, there’s a smart way out of any awkward, uncomfortable or just plain boring conversation. Bernstein calls it the Connect and Close technique, which boils down to being direct and physically following through.

First, you deliver this magical line: “It was really nice to see you—I’m glad we got a chance to catch up. I’m going to go say hello to a few other people.”

At the same time, you pair it with some very specific body language. “You can look across the room, wave to someone or shift and turn your body a little bit away while you’re saying it,” Bernstein says. “Then they’re getting information not only from your words but also from what they’re seeing.”

Then—and this is the part most of us have the most trouble with—you leave.

Why does the Connect and Close work?

Simply put, it’s kind and clear. “You’re acknowledging the time that you spent with them, but then also being direct and moving on,” Bernstein says. Because there’s no ambiguity, the other person isn’t left wondering what just happened. Plus, says Mastroianni, you make the other person feel appreciated, not that you’re “simply fed up with their presence.”

In fact, it’s the long, apologetic exit that’s more likely to sting. “When it’s indirect or there’s too much talking, it gives people room to start thinking, Wait a second—they seem really uncomfortable. Don’t they want to talk to me?”  Bernstein says. “If they don’t have that space, they don’t have that thought.”

And if you’re worried that cutting things short will hurt someone’s feelings, the research suggests otherwise. “Going in [to our study], we expected that if a conversation ended before someone wanted it to end, they’d feel pretty bummed. This is not what we found,” Mastroianni says. “If anything, they were the happiest group! It turns out it’s fine to be left wanting more.” His analogy: “Think about finishing a bowl of ice cream: If you want more ice cream, it’s probably because the ice cream was pretty good. If you want less ice cream, it’s probably because your stomach hurts.”

What shouldn’t you do when ending a conversation?

Even with the right words, a few common slip-ups can make the exit more awkward than it needs to be. Here’s what to avoid.

  • Ending with a question. This is the biggest mistake people make, according to Bernstein. “They’ll say, ‘It was so great to catch up. I’m going to go grab a drink—is that OK with you?’ And then we keep ourselves in the conversation [with] an additional question, because we feel bad.”
  • Putting the exit on the other person. Saying something like “I’m sure you have lots of people you want to talk to” feels gracious, but it’s really a way to get them to leave so you don’t have to feel bad. “That can backfire,” Bernstein says. “They could say, ‘No, I’m good, actually.’ And then what do you do?”
  • Being too nice. Gushing on your way out by saying something like “We should totally get lunch!” only confuses the message, says Zohar. “Don’t make a promise to somebody that you don’t plan on delivering.” And remember: You don’t owe anyone a reason either.

How can you tweak the Connect and Close for different situations?

The basic formula works almost anywhere with anyone, but a few small adjustments can help.

At a family gathering: If you’re settled in on the couch, Bernstein says, simply stand up after you deliver the line. Try something like: “It was so good to chat with you. I’m going to go see how Aunt Sally’s doing—I haven’t talked to her in a while.”

When a relative gets nosy: That aunt who wants to know why you’re still single? You don’t owe her an explanation. Zohar suggests turning the spotlight around: “That’s not something I’m comfortable sharing, but let’s talk about you. Tell me about your trip.” It works, she says, because “people love to talk about themselves.”

At a work event: Offer a handshake along with something like: “It was good to see you again. Take care, and have fun tonight,” Bernstein suggests.

With a friend who’s venting: You don’t want to seem dismissive when someone is clearly going through something. Acknowledge what they’re sharing, then suggest a time to continue. “You could say, ‘It certainly sounds like there’s a lot going on. I really do want to hear about it, but unfortunately I have to go. Maybe we can catch up again soon and you can fill me in,'” Bernstein suggests. And if you’re two martinis into your friend’s breakup story, Zohar says it’s OK to validate what they’re going through, then be honest that you don’t have the bandwidth right now. Her take: “Honesty is kindness, and I think a lot of people are scared of that.”

When you truly can’t leave: At a seated holiday dinner, you may not be able to walk across the room. Bernstein recommends having a helpful exit ready, such as: “I’m going to start on the dishes.” Or borrow Zohar’s go-to: “Excuse me for a moment. I’m going to go use the restroom.” Chances are, by the time you return, they’ll have found someone else to unload on. And if someone brings up politics or your love life and you’re stuck at the table? Try to pivot with “I think we’ve talked about that enough—how are you doing?”

Should you reconnect with that person later?

You don’t need to avoid them for the rest of the night. If you cross paths again, Bernstein advises keeping it light: “Hey, how are you? Are you having fun tonight?”

If you’re worried about getting pulled right back into an intense conversation, it’s helpful if you take the wheel. Bernstein says her husband, who’s also a psychologist, is a pro at this. He’ll gently shift things to something neutral, like sports teams, holiday travel plans or what everyone’s watching on Netflix. “It’s something more benign that is still a conversation,” she says, “but it doesn’t suck you into that heaviness where people want to share their whole life story with us.”

That said, you can pick the conversation back up later if you want to. As Mastroianni says, “We always have the option of speaking more in the future, but we never have the option of speaking less than we already did.”

What other phrases and techniques should you have in your arsenal?

The Connect and Close should be your go-to, but it helps to have a few backup moves ready, especially when the usual exit isn’t an option.

  • “I’m going to see if anyone needs a hand in the kitchen.” Volunteering for a task, which Bernstein recommends, gives you a built-in reason to leave—and makes you look like the most helpful guest in the room.
  • “Excuse me for a moment. It was great to talk to you.” Zohar’s go-to is short and sweet, and it doesn’t require an explanation.
  • “I really want to hear more—let’s catch up another time?” Bernstein’s rain check tells a friend that you care about what they’re sharing, even though now isn’t the time to talk.
  • “It’s past my bedtime. It was great to meet you, and I hope you have a great night.” Stuck next to someone at a dinner party? An honest end-of-night exit, which Zohar has used herself, works when there’s no room to roam.
  • Wave to someone across the room. Even a small gesture signals that you’re about to move on, so your exit line doesn’t come out of nowhere, Bernstein says.

How can you make sure you’re not holding someone hostage?

It happens to the best of us, especially when we’re excited about what we’re saying. Bernstein suggests checking for these signs that the other person is ready to move on.

  • Are they making eye contact or looking around the room?
  • Are they shifting their weight or taking a step back?
  • Are they pulling out their phone?
  • Are they asking questions and contributing or just saying “Yeah,” “Uh-huh” and “Sure”?
  • Does it feel like it’s more of a dialogue rather than a reporting session?
  • Are you talking to them or at them?

If you suspect you’ve overstayed your welcome—or you want to avoid that possibility—try these moves.

  • Just ask. If you’re not sure, check in. “Hey, are you still interested in having this conversation? Like, are you still good?” Zohar suggests. And if they say something like “I’m so sorry, my mom is calling,” take the hint and then say, “Oh, no worries—go deal with what you need to deal with.”
  • Use the Connect and Close yourself. “You could say something like ‘I’ve taken up more than enough of your time. I’ll let you get on to the rest of the party,'” Bernstein suggests. The key is to physically move away too, so they aren’t stuck deciding whether to end it. “Some people feel uncomfortable, and they may say, ‘Oh, no, you’re fine!'” she says. “But if you still stay there, then it’s just going to continue.”
  • Give them an opening. Mastroianni calls this offering a “conversational doorknob.” Say something that makes it easy for the other person to jump in, instead of talking at them while they nod along. Ask a question they’ll enjoy answering rather than one that gets a one-word reply. Or share an opinion they can react to, instead of recapping every scene of a movie they haven’t seen. If they have something to say back, you’re having a conversation, not giving a lecture. And if they don’t take the bait? That’s a good sign it’s time to wrap things up.

But wait—does every conversation really need an escape hatch?

No. But if it feels like you’re itching to get away from everyone you talk to, Mastroianni suggests turning the lens on yourself. “Are you being a good conversation partner? Are you paying attention? Are you looking for what’s interesting about the other person?” he says. “Some people are bores, sure, and for those folks, you’ll have to politely excuse yourself eventually. But anyone can be made boring by the way you treat them.”

His research also suggests that our dread is often overblown. Most of the conversations in his study were highly enjoyable to both people, even when they didn’t end sooner. “People are way too anxious about their conversations,” he says. “Over and over again, we find that people fear them beforehand, enjoy them while they’re going on and then completely forget and go back to fearing them again.”

articles.title: Holiday Travel Hack! This Viral Packing Trick Will Help You Flatten Your Bulky Sweaters and Fit More in Your Bag
articles.content:
Between overstuffed suitcases and the possibility of your luggage taking an entirely different holiday vacation than you, traveling around Thanksgiving and Christmas can feel like a lot. As someone who travels frequently, I’ve learned a thing or two about packing smarter, especially when it comes to squeezing more into my suitcase without having to check an extra bag. So when a clever luggage hack that promised to maximize packing space started making the rounds on Instagram and racked up more than 2 million views, you better believe I was intrigued.
But does this viral packing trick to flatten those bulky sweaters and use every ounce of space in your suitcase actually live up to the hype? You’re about to find out. I also spoke with travel expert and Emmy-winning TV host Samantha Brown for her take on it, along with a few other packing tips worth remembering.
Read on to find out how to make your next trip a little less stressful.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more travel, holiday tips, fun facts, humor, cleaning and tech all week long.
View this post on Instagram
This viral packing trick is twofold: It makes use of an often-overlooked space in your suitcase and involves folding your bulkier clothes a little differently to maximize room. First, you know those awkward gaps between the raised rails at the bottom of your suitcase? Instead of piling your clothes on top and leaving that valuable space unused, fill in those grooves with smaller clothing items, like T-shirts and scarves. Make sure you fold them to match the size of the gaps.
Then, lay the rest of your clothes flat on top to create even layers. Bulky sweaters? Place them flat rather than folding or rolling them to cut down on volume. Jeans? Fold them twice to help maintain their shape without taking up unnecessary room. As for shoes, those go on the other side of your suitcase.
“Overall, your goal is to eliminate pockets of space caused by putting rolled or folded bulkier layers on top,” says Brown. “That’s wasted space.” Plus, laying clothes flat may help minimize wrinkles. (More on that below.)
While there’s no exact percentage for how much extra space this packing hack saves, the results in the viral video are pretty impressive. Using what she describes as being a medium-to-large suitcase, the creator manages to fit three bulky sweaters, three pairs of jeans and several long-sleeve shirts, with plenty of room left over for more. Depending on how the pieces are mixed and matched, that could be enough clothing for roughly three to five days of outfits, even before adding anything else.
For comparison, a typical medium suitcase (24 to 27 inches depending on the brand) can hold about five to seven or more days’ worth of clothing, while a large suitcase (around 28 to 32 inches) can accommodate seven to 14 or more days, depending on how bulky the clothes are and how much room shoes and toiletries take up.
So while it’s hard to say exactly how many additional outfits this method could accommodate, the video suggests it could be a useful trick for travelers looking to pack more without upgrading to a larger suitcase. But remember, your results will depend on the size of your luggage and the types of clothes you’re bringing.
Before you completely rethink your packing routine, there are a few things worth considering. For starters, folding clothes flat doesn’t guarantee they’ll arrive wrinkle-free, especially if your suitcase is packed tightly. Brown has one suggestion for getting ahead of this potential problem: “The only thing I would have done differently is put the blazer at the very top or after the heavier items like the pants to prevent deep-set wrinkles.”
Another potential issue? Finding what you need once you arrive. “There’s zero organization because it’s all about packing as much as you can,” Brown points out. “You’ll need to completely unpack to get to anything, and you may need that sweater.” So if you’re someone who prefers living out of their suitcase rather than unpacking at the hotel, this method might not be your favorite. My advice? Keep anything you’ll want right away near the top.
All of this being said, just because you can fit more into your suitcase, it doesn’t mean you should. Extra clothes can quickly add extra weight, so keep your airline’s baggage limits in mind before getting too carried away. After all, saving space won’t feel like much of a win if you’re hit with an overweight-bag fee at the airport.
Even if you’ve mastered the art of fitting everything into your suitcase, a few overlooked packing mistakes could still throw a wrench in your holiday travel plans. Here’s what you need to know.

Even if you’ve mastered the art of fitting everything into your suitcase, a few overlooked packing mistakes could still throw a wrench in your holiday travel plans. Here’s what you need to know.

  • Be strategic about how many pants you pack. According to Brown, pants add the most weight and take up the most room. “Make sure the pants you bring can be worn three times,” she says. “If you’re going away for seven days, two pairs of pants will actually give you six wears.”
  • Wear your bulkiest clothes on the plane. “Your boots, sweaters and jackets should all be worn and never packed,” Brown says. That’s one way to free up some much-needed suitcase space.
  • Leave room for holiday gifts. If you’re visiting family or friends, don’t pack your suitcase to the brim on the way there. Between presents and last-minute shopping finds, you might come home with more than you brought. And yes, I’m definitely guilty of this!
  • Plan outfits instead of packing options. I’m all for having choices, but bringing five sweaters for a three-day Thanksgiving trip? Probably unnecessary. Try planning outfits you can mix and match so you’re not packing half your closet for a long weekend.
  • Use your carry-on’s expandable feature to your advantage. “When you’re packing a carry-on, always expand the bag first,” says Brown. “Pack it all the way to the top, then zip it up. Zipping it up gives you the benefit of compression while not exceeding the size limits of the airline.”
  • Don’t wrap your Christmas presents before flying. Yep, seriously! If TSA needs to inspect a gift in your carry-on or checked bag, agents may have to unwrap it, and all that pretty wrapping paper could go to waste. Save yourself the hassle by packing gifts in gift bags or wrapping them once you arrive at your destination.
